{{Short description|Cryptographical test for pseudo-randomness}}
In [[cryptography]] and the [[theory of computation]], '''Yao's test''' is a test defined by [[Andrew Chi-Chih Yao]] in 1982,<ref name="yao82">[[Andrew Chi-Chih Yao]]. [https://www.di.ens.fr/users/phan/secuproofs/yao82.pdf Theory and applications of trapdoor functions]. In Proceedings of the 23rd IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, 1982.</ref> against pseudo-random sequences. A sequence of words passes Yao's test if an attacker with reasonable computational power cannot distinguish it from a sequence generated uniformly at random.

== Formal statement ==

=== Boolean circuits ===
Let <math>P</math> be a polynomial, and <math>S=\{S_k\}_k</math> be a collection of sets <math>S_k</math> of <math>P(k)</math>-bit long sequences, and for each <math>k</math>, let <math>\mu_k</math> be a [[probability distribution]] on <math>S_k</math>, and <math>P_C</math> be a polynomial. A predicting collection <math>C=\{C_k\}</math> is a collection of [[boolean circuits]] of size less than <math>P_C(k)</math>. Let <math>p_{k,S}^C</math> be the probability that on input <math>s</math>, a string randomly selected in <math>S_k</math> with probability <math>\mu(s)</math>, <math>C_k(s)=1</math>, i.e.

<div style="text-align: center;">
<math>p_{k,S}^C={\mathcal P}[C_k(s)=1 | s\in S_k\text{ with probability }\mu_k(s)]</math>
</div>

Moreover, let <math>p_{k,U}^C</math> be the probability that <math>C_k(s)=1</math> on input <math>s</math> a <math>P(k)</math>-bit long sequence selected [[Uniform distribution (discrete)|uniformly at random]] in <math>\{0,1\}^{P(k)}</math>. We say that <math>S</math> passes Yao's test if for all predicting collection <math>C</math>, for all but finitely many <math>k</math>, for all polynomial <math>Q</math> :

<div style="text-align: center;">
<math>|p_{k,S}^C-p_{k,U}^C|<\frac{1}{Q(k)}</math>
</div>

=== Probabilistic formulation ===
As in the case of the [[next-bit test]], the predicting collection used in the above definition can be replaced by a probabilistic Turing machine, working in polynomial time. This also yields a strictly stronger definition of Yao's test (see [[P/poly#Adleman's theorem|Adleman's theorem]]). Indeed, one could decide [[Undecidable problem|undecidable]] properties of the pseudo-random sequence with the non-uniform circuits described above, whereas [[Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial|BPP]] machines can always be simulated by exponential-time [[Turing machines|deterministic Turing machines]].
